data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"A single evaluation cannot distinguish genuine reliability from checklist coincidence because both produce identical observable outcomes on the items tested; the distinction is a property of the counterfactual distribution over untested items, which a single evaluation cannot access.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the single evaluation includes adversarial or perturbation items, it may approximate access to the counterfactual distribution and the distinction becomes partially observable.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the task domain is so narrow that a single evaluation exhausts it, transfer is not required and the distinction collapses.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If prior knowledge about the checklist's structure (causal vs. correlational) is admitted, it may constrain the counterfactual even without new data.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Genuine reliability and coincidence differ only in how the process would perform on items outside the evaluation set. A single evaluation observes performance on tested items only. If the panel scores well, this is equally consistent with (a) a robust process that would transfer and (b) a fragile process that happened to align. To distinguish them, one must observe performance under perturbation or on held-out items\u2014neither of which is available within a single evaluation. The distinction is therefore epistemically inaccessible without additional data.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
